raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old HIV-infected male patient presented with a 4-week history of burning mouth and dysgeusia that progressed to glossodynia over the course of a few days. A 7-day treatment with fluconazole, followed by a 7-day course of itraconazole, had been offered without clinical improvement. The condition worsened to the point of weight loss and feeding difficulties due to sore throat and odynophagia.
The patient was on successful highly active antiretroviral therapy with lamivudine, tenofovir, and efavirenz for more than 4 years. He reported no prior rash and denied the use of drugs other than his current antiretroviral regimen. There was no evidence of a psychiatric disorder and no major complications of AIDS had ever been recorded. He was a current smoker in otherwise good health. Secondary syphilis had been fully and successfully treated 8 years earlier and previous Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) assays were negative.
Examination of the oral cavity (Figure 1(a)) revealed shallow, painful, round to oval depapillary erosions on a background of a whitish, nonwipeable hyperkeratotic thickening of the posterior aspect of the tongue. This overall aspect shared resemblance with reported cases of syphilitic lesions of the tongue, as well as a sign previously described as plaques en prairie fauchee. A painful split papule was also present in the left oral commissure. This commissural lesion was not a simple fissure as seen in angular cheilitis (perleche). Instead, it was a fibrin-covered commissural papule cleaved in two faces. This sign, previously described as fausse perleche (or false angular cheilitis), is also associated with secondary syphilis. The patient indicated that he had never had such lesions in the past. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy or any tegumentary abnormalities. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.
The CD4 cell count was 995 cells/mm3 and the plasma HIV viral load was consistently below detection limits. A novel VDRL assay was performed and yielded a titer of 1/128. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests were reactive for IgG and IgM. Laboratory evaluations were otherwise unremarkable. On further history taking, the patient indicated having had unprotected oral and anogenital sexual contact approximately 3 months before the onset of symptoms. A complete clinical remission and resolution of oral lesions (Figure 1(b)) was rapidly recorded after the first of a total of three consecutive weekly administrations of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G. A clinical diagnosis of secondary syphilis was then made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old HIV-positive man presented with a 4-week history of burning mouth, dysgeusia, painful tongue erosions (glossodynia), sore throat, odynophagia, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 4 weeks, the patient developed oral burning and altered taste that rapidly progressed to severe glossodynia, sore throat, odynophagia, feeding difficulties, and weight loss, failing consecutive 7-day courses of oral fluconazole and itraconazole.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of well-controlled HIV infection on HAART (lamivudine, tenofovir, and efavirenz) for >4 years with no prior AIDS-defining illnesses. History of secondary syphilis 8 years earlier that had been successfully treated with documented negative follow-up VDRL assays. Current tobacco smoker; upon further questioning, he disclosed unprotected oral and anogenital sexual contact ~3 months before symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for glossodynia, dysgeusia, painful left oral commissure lesion, odynophagia, and weight loss; negative for skin rash. Home medications: lamivudine, tenofovir, and efavirenz; recent ineffective fluconazole and itraconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Intraoral examination revealed shallow, painful, round-to-oval depapillated erosions over a whitish, non-wipeable hyperkeratotic plaque on the posterior dorsal tongue ('plaques en prairie fauchee' / mowed-meadow tongue plaques), plus a painful fibrin-covered split papule at the left oral commissure ('fausse perleche'). There was no cervical lymphadenopathy or cutaneous rash.
objective.routine_investigations: Plasma HIV-1 viral load was undetectable, and routine laboratory panels were unremarkable.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis re-infection presenting exclusively with oral mucosal plaques ('plaques en prairie fauchee') and a left commissural split papule ('fausse perleche'; oral candidiasis excluded by antifungal failure and serology), established via seroconversion to a high-titer serum VDRL (1:128) and reactive FTA-ABS IgG and IgM. Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks, achieving rapid and complete clinical resolution of all oral and commissural lesions after the first injection.
